question_text: Functions $f$ and $g$ are given by $f : x \mapsto e^{x+1}$ and $g : x \mapsto \ln x - 1$.

subparts.stem: Find $(f \circ g)(x)$ and state its domain and range.
subparts.solution:
$(f \circ g)(x) = f(g(x)) = f(\ln x - 1) = e^{(\ln x - 1) + 1} = e^{\ln x} = x$.
The domain is $\{x \mid x > 0\}$.
The range is $\{y \mid y > 0\}$.

ai_explanation.concept_rule: The composite function $(f \circ g)(x) = f(g(x))$. Its domain is restricted by the domain of the inner function $g(x)$. Since $\ln x$ is only defined for $x > 0$, the domain of $(f \circ g)(x)$ is $x > 0$, giving a range of $y > 0$.
step_by_step: Substitute $g(x) = \ln x - 1$ into $f(x) = e^{x+1}$: $f(\ln x - 1) = e^{(\ln x - 1)+1}$.
Simplify the exponent: $\ln x - 1 + 1 = \ln x$, so $e^{\ln x} = x$.
Determine the domain: inner function $\ln x$ requires $x > 0$.
Since $(f \circ g)(x) = x$ for $x > 0$, the range is $y > 0$.
ai_explanation.common_pitfalls: Forgetting that $(f \circ g)(x) = x$ does not have a domain of all real numbers because the inner function $\ln x$ is only defined for $x > 0$.

subparts.stem: Find $(g \circ f)(x)$ and state its domain and range.
subparts.solution:
$(g \circ f)(x) = g(f(x)) = g(e^{x+1}) = \ln(e^{x+1}) - 1 = x + 1 - 1 = x$.
The domain is $\{x \mid x \in \mathbb{R}\}$.
The range is $\{y \mid y \in \mathbb{R}\}$.

ai_explanation.concept_rule: For $(g \circ f)(x) = g(f(x))$, substitute $f(x)$ into $g(x)$. Since $e^{x+1} > 0$ for all real $x$, the logarithm is always well-defined, so the domain is all real numbers.
step_by_step: Substitute $f(x) = e^{x+1}$ into $g(x) = \ln x - 1$ to get $\ln(e^{x+1}) - 1$.
Use the inverse property $\ln(e^u) = u$ to obtain $(x + 1) - 1 = x$.
The inner function $f(x) = e^{x+1}$ is defined for all $x \in \mathbb{R}$ and always positive, so the domain is $\{x \mid x \in \mathbb{R}\}$.
Since $(g \circ f)(x) = x$ over all reals, the range is $\{y \mid y \in \mathbb{R}\}$.
ai_explanation.common_pitfalls: Incorrectly restricting the domain because of the natural log in $g$, ignoring that its input $e^{x+1}$ is strictly positive for all $x$.

subparts.stem: Graph $y = f(x)$ and $y = g(x)$ on the same set of axes.
subparts.final_answer: $Graph showing $y = e^{x+1}$ with horizontal asymptote $y=0$ and intercept $(0,e)$, $y = \ln x - 1$ with vertical asymptote $x=0$ and intercept $(e,0)$, and the line of symmetry $y = x$.$

mark_breakdown.desc: Sketch exponential curve and logarithmic curve
Include line of reflection $y = x$ and label key features

subparts.solution: Sketch of $y = e^{x+1}$, $y = \ln x - 1$, and the line $y = x$ showing reflectional symmetry.

ai_explanation.concept_rule: Inverse functions are reflections of each other across the diagonal line $y = x$.
step_by_step: Plot the curve $y = e^{x+1}$, passing through $(0, e)$ and $(-1, 1)$, with horizontal asymptote $y=0$.
Plot the curve $y = \ln x - 1$, passing through $(e, 0)$ and $(1, -1)$, with vertical asymptote $x=0$.
Draw the dashed line $y = x$ to demonstrate that each curve is a reflection of the other.
ai_explanation.common_pitfalls: Swapping the asymptotes (exponential has horizontal asymptote, logarithmic has vertical asymptote).

subparts.final_answer: $The graph of $y = g(x)$ is a reflection of the graph of $y = f(x)$ in the line $y = x$, so $f$ and $g$ are inverses of one another.$

mark_breakdown.desc: Identify reflection across $y = x$ and conclude that $f$ and $g$ are inverse functions

subparts.solution:
The graph of $y = g(x)$ is a reflection of the graph of $y = f(x)$ in the line $y = x$.
$\therefore f$ and $g$ are inverses of one another.

ai_explanation.concept_rule: Two functions are inverses if and only if their graphs are reflections of one another across the line $y = x$.
step_by_step: Observe that reflecting any point $(a, b)$ on $y = f(x)$ across $y = x$ gives $(b, a)$ on $y = g(x)$.
Conclude that $f$ and $g$ are mutually inverse functions.
ai_explanation.common_pitfalls: Stating that they are inverses without referencing the geometric property of reflection across the line $y = x$.
